# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 21 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 21 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_021_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 3, Chapter 13

**1** "Those from the sixth mountain with its large and small clefts — who are they?" "Those with the small clefts are those who have grievances against one another and are somewhat at odds. Many of them wear themselves out through their disputes, but repentance is open to them, and those who repent will live to God. Those with the large clefts are those who quarrel constantly and nurse lasting ill will against one another. **2** These have been cast out of the tower and rejected. Repentance is difficult for such people, but if they repent they will have a place in the building; if they do not repent, they will perish." **3** "Those from the seventh mountain — the cheerful and flourishing one — these are those who were submissive and gentle and free from quarreling. They always rejoiced in the servants of God, clothed themselves in the Holy Spirit, and showed mercy to everyone. They gave freely from their own resources, without reproach or hesitation." **4** "The Lord therefore sees their simplicity and undivided goodness and fills them with the blessings of his good things. They are worthy of eternal life because of their good character, their innocence, and their labor for the Lord's servants." **5** "Those from the eighth mountain — with its springs where all creatures drank — these are the apostles and teachers who proclaimed to the whole world, teaching the word of the Lord in holiness and truth, holding back from every evil desire and walking always in righteousness and truth. **6** These are always at peace with one another; they are established in peace and will live to God." **7** "Those from the ninth mountain — the wilderness of deadly beasts and serpents — these are the deacons who administered badly; they stole from widows and orphans and profited personally from their ministry. If they persist in this they will die with no hope of life; but if they repent and complete their ministry in purity, life remains open to them." **8** "Those from the tenth mountain — the shaded one where the flocks rested — these are the bishops and those given to hospitality who always welcomed God's servants into their homes with sincere joy. These bishops at all times sheltered the afflicted and the widows in their care and conducted themselves with holiness in all things." **9** "All these will be under the Lord's shelter forever. Those who did these things are glorious before God, and their place is already set among the angels — if they keep the Lord's commandments." **10** "Those from the eleventh mountain — the fruit-bearing one — these are those who suffered for the name of the Lord and surrendered their lives and possessions readily and wholeheartedly, suffering willingly for his name." **11** "Those from the twelfth mountain — the entirely white one — these are the innocent ones, the infants in faith, into whose hearts no evil ever entered. They never knew what wickedness was, and they always remained in childlike innocence." **12** "These will rest forever and live with God without doubt. Blessed are all of you who have cast off wickedness and clothed yourselves with innocence — you will be the first to live to God."

---

### Council Notes

This chapter completes the twelve-mountain typology. The final catalog of mountains 6-12:
- **Mountain 6:** the quarrelsome (minor and chronic)
- **Mountain 7:** the gentle and giving (filled with the Spirit)
- **Mountain 8:** apostles and teachers of the whole world
- **Mountain 9:** corrupt deacons who robbed widows and orphans
- **Mountain 10:** hospitable bishops who sheltered the afflicted
- **Mountain 11:** martyrs
- **Mountain 12:** innocent believers like children

The sequence is not strictly ascending — mountain 9 (corrupt deacons) is inserted between the glorious mountain 8 and 10, a deliberate structural reminder that the church hierarchy contains both the best and worst.

The final beatitude (v. 12) is the climax of the entire Vision section: innocence is the ultimate virtue, and it is available to all who repent. The entire tower-allegory ultimately serves this pastoral call.
